answers.brief_reasoning: Competitive inhibitor structurally resembles substrate and binds the active site, blocking substrate binding, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form per unit time and rate decreases.
answers.final_answer: It binds reversibly to the enzyme's active site (competing with substrate), preventing substrate from binding, reducing the number of enzyme-substrate complexes formed and thus the reaction rate.

answers.brief_reasoning: IV = [compound X]; DV = initial reaction rate. Constants: substrate concentration, enzyme concentration, temperature, pH. Pattern: rate decreases as [X] increases, with diminishing decreases per µM (nonlinear).
answers.final_answer: (i) IV: concentration of compound X (µM); DV: mean initial reaction rate (µmol product/min). (ii) e.g., substrate concentration (or enzyme concentration, temperature, pH). (iii) As concentration of X increases from 0 to 8 µM, the initial rate decreases (39.1 to 12.3 µmol/min); the decline is nonlinear—smaller decrease per µM at higher concentrations.
(i) (12.3 − 39.1)/39.1 × 100 ≈ −68.5% (a 68.5% decrease). (ii) Yes: 2 µM interval 26.26–30.54 and 4 µM interval 18.24–21.96 do not overlap, so the difference is statistically supported.

answers.brief_reasoning: High substrate outcompetes competitive inhibitor for active site, so inhibition is reduced.
answers.final_answer: Compound X's inhibitory effect would be reduced (rates at each [X] closer to the uninhibited rate, which would approach Vmax), because the much more abundant substrate outcompetes X for the active site, so substrate binds most active sites.

answers.brief_reasoning: Definition: water potential (Ψ = Ψs + Ψp) measures how much potential energy water has per unit volume, which sets how free it is to move. Water moves by osmosis.
answers.final_answer: Water potential (Ψ = Ψs + Ψp) is the potential energy of water per unit volume compared with pure water at atmospheric pressure. It shows how likely water is to move. Net water movement is from higher (less negative) water potential to lower (more negative) water potential.

answers.brief_reasoning: Use a line graph because the independent variable is continuous. The points fall on a straight line.
answers.final_answer: Line graph: x-axis 'Sucrose molarity (M)' from 0 to 1.0. y-axis 'Percent change in mass (%)' from about -25 to +10, with a zero line. Plot all 6 points, connect them or draw a best-fit line (slope -28% per M, y-intercept 7%), and add a title.

answers.brief_reasoning: The data are linear: % change = 7 − 28M. Setting this to 0 gives M = 0.25. The x-intercept falls between 0.2 M (+1.4%) and 0.4 M (−4.2%).
answers.final_answer: (i) About 0.25 M sucrose (any value from about 0.2 to 0.3 M is acceptable). (ii) Null hypothesis: sucrose molarity has no effect on the percent change in mass of the potato cores.

answers.brief_reasoning: Ψs = −iCRT. NaCl has i = 2, so 0.4 M NaCl has about the same solute effect as 0.8 M sucrose.
answers.final_answer: The cores would lose more mass, giving a more negative percent change (about −15% instead of −4.2%). NaCl splits into 2 ions, so the number of solute particles doubles (i = 2). This makes the solute potential and the solution's water potential more negative, so more water leaves the cores by osmosis.

answers.brief_reasoning: Water moves from higher to lower water potential.
answers.final_answer: There is a net movement of water out of the cell into the solution, because water moves from higher water potential (inside the cell) to lower water potential (outside). The cell loses water and mass, and in plant cells the membrane pulls away from the wall (plasmolysis).

Distilled water has a water potential of 0, which is higher than the negative water potential of the potato cells. So there is a net movement of water into the cells by osmosis until the cell wall's pressure stops further uptake.

answers.brief_reasoning: ETC passes electrons from NADH/FADH2 down a series of carriers to O2 (final acceptor, forming water), using the released energy to pump H+ from the matrix into the intermembrane space, which builds an electrochemical gradient used to make ATP.
answers.final_answer: The ETC carries electrons from NADH and FADH2 to O2, which forms water. The energy released is used to pump H+ into the intermembrane space, making a proton gradient that powers ATP synthesis (oxidative phosphorylation).

answers.brief_reasoning: H+ moves down its gradient through ATP synthase, which makes the enzyme rotate. The rotation changes the enzyme's shape so it joins ADP and Pi.
answers.final_answer: Protons move down their electrochemical gradient (intermembrane space to matrix) through ATP synthase. This flow makes part of the enzyme rotate, and the resulting shape changes join ADP + Pi to make ATP (chemiosmosis).

answers.brief_reasoning: Electron flow stops, so oxidative phosphorylation stops.
answers.final_answer: Mitochondrial ATP production drops sharply, nearly to zero. Only a small amount would still come from the Krebs cycle (substrate-level), and that also stops once NAD+ runs out.

answers.brief_reasoning: With no electron flow, no H+ is pumped. The gradient dissipates, so ATP synthase has no proton-motive force to drive it.
answers.final_answer: Because electrons cannot pass to O2, the chain backs up and the proton pumps stop moving H+ into the intermembrane space. The proton gradient is no longer kept up and runs down, so there is no H+ flow through ATP synthase and no ATP is made.

answers.brief_reasoning: The fork moves left, so the leading strand has to grow leftward. A strand that grows leftward has its 3' end on the left, so it pairs with a template that runs 5' on the left to 3' on the right. That is the top strand.
answers.final_answer: Top template strand

answers.brief_reasoning: DNA polymerase only adds nucleotides to a free 3' end, so new DNA is made 5'→3'. On the bottom template, that direction points away from the moving fork. The polymerase therefore has to keep starting again near the fork, using new RNA primers. It makes short Okazaki fragments, which DNA ligase later joins together.
answers.final_answer: The new strand on the bottom template is made 5'→3', which is away from the fork. So it is made in short Okazaki fragments, each started with a new primer, and these are later joined by ligase.

answers.brief_reasoning: Pair each base of the top strand, GACGCTAA, with its complement. The new strand runs antiparallel to the top strand, so its left end is 3' and its right end is 5'.
answers.final_answer: 3'-CTGCGATT-5'

answers.brief_reasoning: The two strands run in opposite directions. DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3' end, so it reads the template 3'→5' and builds the new strand 5'→3'. As a result, one new strand (the leading strand) is made continuously toward the fork. The other (the lagging strand) is made in fragments away from the fork. Each new strand is antiparallel to its template, and replication is semiconservative.
answers.final_answer: Because the strands are antiparallel and polymerase only builds 5'→3', the two strands are copied differently. The leading strand is made continuously and the lagging strand is made in Okazaki fragments.

answers.brief_reasoning: The rate goes up from pH 4 to pH 7 and then down at pH 10.
answers.final_answer: The reaction rate is highest at pH 7 (18.2 µmol/min). It is lower at pH 10 (9.1 µmol/min) and lowest at pH 4 (5.9 µmol/min). So the rate rises from pH 4 to pH 7 and then falls at pH 10.

answers.final_answer: The claim is supported among the pH values tested. The ±2SE range at pH 7 (16.32–20.08) does not overlap with the range at pH 4 (5.24–6.56) or pH 10 (8.42–9.78), so the rate at pH 7 is significantly higher than at the other two. answers.brief_reasoning: A low pH changes the charges on amino acid R groups, which disrupts the enzyme's shape.
answers.final_answer: At pH 4 there are extra H+ ions. These change the charges (ionization) on the enzyme's amino acid side chains, which disrupts the hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold its 3-D shape. The active site changes shape or charge (partial denaturation), so less substrate binds and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form. This makes the rate lower than at pH 7, where the enzyme keeps its normal shape.
